You said:

I currently use sin/cos to transfer an arbitrary dir value into a vector. export function toXY(speed, angle) { let x = speed * Math.sin(angle) let y = speed * Math.cos(angle) return(new Vector(x, y)) } My only question is, what angle would be up (0 x and -1 y) and is increasing dir going left or decreasing dir going left

ChatGPT said:

Good question—this is exactly where coordinate-system intuition matters, and your current function is not using the standard mapping, which is why it’s confusing.

🚨 First: your current function

TypeScript
let x = speed * Math.sin(angle)
let y = speed * Math.cos(angle)

This effectively means:

  • 0° → (0, +1) → down

  • angles increase → rotate clockwise

  • it's rotated 90° compared to the usual math convention

📍 What angle is “up” (0, -1)?

Let’s solve it directly from your formula:

We want:

x = 0
y = -1

So:

sin(angle) = 0
cos(angle) = -1

That happens at:

👉 angle = π radians (180°)

📍 Direction of increasing angle

Let’s test a few angles:

anglex = siny = cosdirection
0°0+1down
90°+10right
180°0-1up
270°-10left

✅ Conclusion

  • Up (0, -1) → 180°

  • Left (-1, 0) → 270°

  • Increasing angle rotates clockwise

  • So:

    • increasing → right → up → left

    • decreasing → right → down → left

👉 Left is reached by increasing angle (toward 270°)

⚠️ Why this feels weird

Standard game/math convention is usually:

TypeScript
x = cos(angle)
y = sin(angle)

But you swapped them.

✅ Recommended version (less confusing)

TypeScript
export function toXY(speed, angle) {
    let x = speed * Math.cos(angle)
    let y = speed * Math.sin(angle)
    return new Vector(x, y)
}

Then you get:

angledirection
0°right
90°down (in Excalibur.js)
180°left
270°up

🧠 If you want “0 = up” (common in top-down games)

Use this instead:

TypeScript
let x = speed * Math.sin(angle)
let y = -speed * Math.cos(angle)

Then:

  • 0° → up

  • 90° → right

  • 180° → down

  • 270° → left

🎯 Bottom line for YOUR current code

  • Up = 180°

  • Left = 270°

  • Increasing angle turns clockwise

  • Left is reached by increasing angle

If you tell me which orientation your sprites use (facing right vs up), I can give you the exact formula so rotation + movement + visuals all line up perfectly.

You said:

My nugget brain forgot that toXY takes a speed and angle input, not just angle input. Anyways, what is the range on friction? is it 0-1 with 0 being no friction and 1 being unmovable, or is it the higher the less movable, etc

ChatGPT said:

In Excalibur.js, body.friction is not a 0–1 “hard clamp” slider, and it’s also not “higher = less movable”.

It behaves like a physics coefficient of friction, similar to Box2D-style models.

🧠 What friction actually means

TypeScript
this.body.friction = 0.5;

It controls how much tangential velocity is reduced during contact between two bodies.

So it only matters when:

  • the actor is in contact with something else

  • or sliding along another collider

📊 Practical range (what actually works)

Even though it’s technically unbounded, in practice:

✅ Typical values

  • 0 → no surface friction (slippery, ice-like)

  • 0.1 – 0.3 → very slippery (fish / floating feel)

  • 0.4 – 0.8 → normal “ground” feel

  • 1.0 → high friction (stops sliding quickly)

⚠️ Above 1.0

  • can behave “sticky”

  • may feel like objects lock together

  • not usually recommended unless you want glue-like behavior

🚨 Key misconception to fix

“1 = unmovable”

❌ Not correct.

Friction does NOT prevent movement.

It only affects:

  • sliding along surfaces

  • how quickly tangential velocity decays during contact

🐟 For your fish/enemy setup

Since you're doing AI movement:

If fish should feel floaty:

TypeScript
this.body.friction = 0.05;

If fish should slightly resist clustering:

TypeScript
this.body.friction = 0.2;

If you’re seeing jitter in crowding:

Lower friction first before touching anything else.

🧠 What actually controls “difficulty to move”

These are the real levers:

1. Mass

TypeScript
this.body.mass

→ affects impulse response

2. Velocity / acceleration (AI logic)

→ most important for enemies

3. Linear damping (VERY important for your case)

TypeScript
this.body.linearDamping = 0.5;

This is often what people think friction does.

  • higher = slows down movement over time

  • great for smoothing fish motion

🎯 Quick rule of thumb

PropertyWhat it actually affects
frictionsliding against other objects
masshow hard it is to accelerate
linearDampinghow quickly movement slows naturally

🚀 Recommendation for your fish system

For smooth “schooling” enemies:

TypeScript
this.body.friction = 0.1;
this.body.linearDamping = 0.3;
this.body.mass = 1;

Then control behavior purely via velocity/steering.

What you’re seeing is almost always caused by one (or more) of these three issues, not the impulse system being random.

In Excalibur.js terms, applyImpulse is deterministic — if it looks random, your input vector is unstable.

🧨 1. You are probably normalizing incorrectly (or not at all)

If your toXY() is:

TypeScript
x = speed * sin(angle)
y = speed * cos(angle)

then the magnitude is already “speed”.

But then you do:

TypeScript
temp.x *= 10
temp.y *= 10
this.body.applyImpulse(temp);

👉 That means:

  • impulse magnitude depends heavily on angle math quirks

  • small floating-point differences become huge jumps

So it looks random, but it’s actually unstable scaling

🧠 2. Your angle function likely flips quadrants unpredictably

If angleToTgt() uses something like atan2, then:

  • correct version: atan2(dy, dx)

  • swapped version: flips left/right unpredictably

Even a small mistake causes:

  • correct direction sometimes

  • opposite direction other times (depending on sign)

That produces exactly your symptom:

“sometimes shoots toward player, sometimes away”

⚠️ 3. You are applying impulse every update tick (accumulation chaos)

If you do:

TypeScript
applyImpulse(temp)

every frame or frequently:

  • impulses stack

  • velocity grows uncontrollably

  • collisions + damping + mass distort direction

Result:

“random rocket behavior”

🧪 4. Debug check (do this first)

Log this BEFORE applying impulse:

TypeScript
console.log({
    player: this.scene?.PLAYER?.pos,
    self: this.pos,
    impulse: temp
});

If you see:

  • NaN

  • undefined

  • wildly changing vectors

→ your math upstream is broken

🧠 5. The real fix (stop using impulse for AI movement)

For steering behavior in Excalibur, impulse is the wrong tool.

Use velocity:

TypeScript
move() {
    const player = this.scene?.PLAYER;
    if (!player) return;

    const angle = angleToTgt(this.pos, player.pos);
    const dir = toXY(1, angle);

    this.vel = dir.scale(150);
}

This removes:

  • physics accumulation noise

  • randomness from damping

  • instability from mass/friction

🚨 Why impulse feels “random” in your case

You’re combining:

  • scaled trig vector ✔

  • physics integration ✔

  • repeated impulses ✔

  • damping ✔

  • collisions ✔

That combination creates:

emergent chaotic motion, not deterministic steering

🎯 If you insist on impulse (correct version)

Then you must do:

You said:

how would I flip the angletoTGT result?

ChatGPT said:

If your angleToTgt() is giving you the opposite direction, you don’t need to “fight” it with hacks—you just invert the vector or flip the angle cleanly.

In Excalibur.js terms, there are three correct ways to flip a direction depending on what you actually mean.

🧭 1. Simplest: flip the vector (recommended)

If you already compute a direction vector:

TypeScript
const dir = player.pos.sub(this.pos);

To reverse it:

TypeScript
const flipped = dir.negate();

or:

TypeScript
const flipped = dir.scale(-1);

👉 This is the cleanest and least error-prone method.

🔁 2. Flip the angle (if you insist on angles)

If angleToTgt() returns an angle in radians:

Reverse direction:

TypeScript
const flippedAngle = angle + Math.PI;

Then:

TypeScript
const dir = toXY(1, flippedAngle);

Why + π works

  • π radians = 180°

  • adding 180° points exactly opposite

⚠️ 3. If your system uses degrees

Then:

TypeScript
flippedAngle = (angle + 180) % 360;

🧠 4. Important warning (your current architecture)

You are mixing:

  • angle-based steering (angleToTgt)

  • trig reconstruction (toXY)

  • physics impulses

That combo is where most “random direction” bugs come from.

If anything feels off, vector math always beats angle math in Excalibur.

🎯 Best recommendation for your case

Since you're using impulse-based “advance behavior”:

👉 do NOT flip angles at all

Just do:

TypeScript
const impulse = player.pos.sub(this.pos).normalize().scale(-strength);

or forward:

TypeScript
const impulse = player.pos.sub(this.pos).normalize().scale(strength);

🧩 Mental model

  • angle = “how rotated is it?”

  • vector = “which direction do I actually move?”

For physics gameplay, vector wins almost every time.

You said:

I mean inverting an angle around a point, so 90 would become 270, 181 would be 179

ChatGPT said:

What you’re describing is a 180° rotation (direction inversion in angle space), not a reflection around a point in world space.

In Excalibur.js terms, this is purely arithmetic on the angle value.

🧭 Invert an angle (correct rule)

If your angle is in degrees:

TypeScript
function invertAngleDeg(a: number) {
    return (a + 180) % 360;
}

If your angle is in radians (very likely in Excalibur):

TypeScript
function invertAngleRad(a: number) {
    return a + Math.PI;
}

🧠 Why this works

You are rotating the direction vector by exactly 180°:

  • 90° → 270° ✔

  • 181° → 1° ✔ (wraps correctly with modulo)

  • π/2 → 3π/2 ✔

⚠️ Important subtlety (this is where most bugs happen)

This only works correctly if:

your angle is already in a consistent coordinate system

If your angle comes from:

TypeScript
Math.atan2(dy, dx)

Then:

  • 0 = right

  • π/2 = down or up depending on Y-axis inversion

So inversion is still correct, but “visual expectation” may feel flipped.

🎯 Practical Excalibur usage

If you’re doing:

TypeScript
const angle = angleToTgt(a, b);

Then invert:

TypeScript
const opposite = angle + Math.PI;
const dir = toXY(speed, opposite);

🧠 Alternative (often better than angle inversion)

Instead of flipping angles:

TypeScript
const dir = a.sub(b).normalize();
const opposite = dir.scale(-1);

This avoids:

  • wrap bugs

  • degree/radian confusion

  • sin/cos mismatch issues

🚀 Rule of thumb

GoalBest method
“Go opposite direction”vector.negate()
“Work in angles anyway”angle + π
“Avoid bugs entirely”vector math only

If you want, I can help you fix your whole movement system so you never have to think in angles again (your current bugs are exactly what happens when angle + physics + impulses mix).

You said:

How do I normalize the vector so that the impulse received is constant no matter the distance? currently it just plugs the distance in the impulse

ChatGPT said:

What you’re seeing is correct physics behavior: if you use the raw vector from A → B, its length is the distance, so your impulse scales with distance.

To make impulse strength constant, you need to normalize the direction vector.

In Excalibur.js, Vector already provides this.

✅ The fix: normalize before scaling

Current (distance affects strength)

TypeScript
const dir = player.pos.sub(this.pos);
this.body.applyImpulse(dir);

Correct (constant strength)

TypeScript
const dir = player.pos.sub(this.pos).normalize();
const impulse = dir.scale(50);

this.body.applyImpulse(impulse);

🧠 What normalization does

Before:

dir = (dx, dy) where magnitude = distance

After:

normalize(dir) → (dx, dy) where magnitude = 1

So now:

  • direction is preserved ✔

  • distance no longer affects strength ✔

⚠️ Important detail (why yours felt chaotic)

Without normalization:

  • far enemies get huge impulse

  • close enemies get tiny impulse

  • behavior becomes “gravity-like pull”

With normalization:

  • every enemy has identical thrust toward target

🎯 Optional: add controlled falloff (better AI feel)

If you want distance to matter slightly (recommended for game feel):

TypeScript
const dir = player.pos.sub(this.pos);
const distance = dir.size;

const normalized = dir.normalize();
const strength = Math.min(distance, 100); // clamp influence

this.body.applyImpulse(normalized.scale(strength * 0.5));

This gives:

  • far enemies stronger push

  • but capped (no explosions)

🧠 Rule of thumb

GoalMethod
constant forcenormalize().scale(constant)
distance-based forceraw vector
controlled AI feelnormalize + clamped distance

You said:

how can I check if I need to use the up down left or right sprite using the dx and dy

ChatGPT said:

You want to convert a direction vector (dx, dy) into a cardinal direction (up/down/left/right) for sprite selection. This is a standard “dominant axis” problem.

In Excalibur.js terms, you’re classifying a vector based on its largest absolute component.

🧠 Core idea

Given:

TypeScript
dx = target.x - current.x
dy = target.y - current.y

You decide direction by asking:

Is horizontal movement stronger or vertical movement stronger?

✅ Clean solution (dominant axis)

TypeScript
function getDirection(dx: number, dy: number) {
    if (Math.abs(dx) > Math.abs(dy)) {
        return dx > 0 ? "right" : "left";
    } else {
        return dy > 0 ? "down" : "up";
    }
}

🧠 Why this works

  • |dx| > |dy| → horizontal movement dominates → left/right

  • otherwise → vertical movement dominates → up/down

So diagonal movement always snaps to the stronger axis.

🎯 Usage example

TypeScript
const dir = player.pos.sub(this.pos);

const facing = getDirection(dir.x, dir.y);

switch (facing) {
    case "left":
        this.graphics.use(Resources.FishLeft.toSprite());
        break;
    case "right":
        this.graphics.use(Resources.FishRight.toSprite());
        break;
    case "up":
        this.graphics.use(Resources.FishUp.toSprite());
        break;
    case "down":
        this.graphics.use(Resources.FishDown.toSprite());
        break;
}

⚡ Alternative: angle-based version (more stable for animations)

If you already compute angles:

TypeScript
function getDirectionFromAngle(angle: number) {
    const deg = (angle * 180) / Math.PI;

    if (deg >= -45 && deg < 45) return "right";
    if (deg >= 45 && deg < 135) return "down";
    if (deg >= -135 && deg < -45) return "up";
    return "left";
}

🧠 Which should you use?

MethodBest for
dx/dy comparisonsimple AI + top-down games
angle-basedsmooth rotation systems
vector angle interpolationadvanced animation blending

🚨 Common mistake (important)

Don’t do this:

TypeScript
if (dx > 0) right else left

That ignores vertical movement and causes:

  • wrong sprite when moving diagonally

  • jittery animation switching

🚀 If you want next step

I can help you upgrade this into:

  • smooth animation blending (no snapping)

  • 8-direction movement (diagonals included)

  • or full angle-driven sprite rotation system

Right now you’re at the point where movement + animation start merging into a proper character controller.


You said:

worky worky, now how can I get enemies to spawn offscreen?

ChatGPT said:

To spawn enemies offscreen in Excalibur.js, you need to sample a position outside the current camera viewport, then optionally randomize which edge they appear on.

There are two solid patterns.

🧭 Option 1: Spawn just outside the camera bounds (recommended)

You use the camera’s world bounds and push the spawn position outward.

TypeScript
function getOffscreenPosition(engine) {
    const cam = engine.currentScene.camera;
    const view = cam.viewport;

    const padding = 50; // how far outside screen

    const left = cam.pos.x - view.width / 2 - padding;
    const right = cam.pos.x + view.width / 2 + padding;
    const top = cam.pos.y - view.height / 2 - padding;
    const bottom = cam.pos.y + view.height / 2 + padding;

    const side = Math.floor(Math.random() * 4);

    switch (side) {
        case 0: return new Vector(left, randomInRange(top, bottom));   // left
        case 1: return new Vector(right, randomInRange(top, bottom));  // right
        case 2: return new Vector(randomInRange(left, right), top);    // top
        default: return new Vector(randomInRange(left, right), bottom);// bottom
    }
}

Then:

TypeScript
const pos = getOffscreenPosition(engine);
const enemy = new EnemyBase(pos);
scene.add(enemy);

🧠 Why this works

You’re explicitly spawning relative to:

  • camera center (cam.pos)

  • viewport size

  • padding buffer

So enemies always start:

just outside what the player can see

🎯 Option 2: Random angle spawn (more organic feel)

Instead of edges, spawn in a ring around the camera:

TypeScript
function getOffscreenRing(engine, radius = 500) {
    const cam = engine.currentScene.camera;

    const angle = Math.random() * Math.PI * 2;

    return new Vector(
        cam.pos.x + Math.cos(angle) * radius,
        cam.pos.y + Math.sin(angle) * radius
    );
}

🐟 When to use which

MethodFeel
edge spawningpredictable waves, arcade feel
ring spawningnatural swarm / fish / ambient AI

🚨 Common mistake

Don’t use world coordinates like:

TypeScript
randomInRange(0, 500)

because once the camera moves:

  • enemies spawn on-screen

  • or too far away to matter

🚀 Bonus: spawn direction toward player

If you want enemies to enter toward the player:

TypeScript
const pos = getOffscreenPosition(engine);
enemy.pos = pos;

const dir = player.pos.sub(pos).normalize();
enemy.body.vel = dir.scale(50);

If you want next step, I can help you build a wave spawner system (timed spawns, difficulty scaling, and edge pressure control).

ChatGPT said:

Short answer: no, you can’t change Math.sin / Math.cos to use degrees. JavaScript is hardwired to radians.

But you can make it feel like degrees with a tiny wrapper (which is what most people do).

✅ Clean solution: degree-friendly trig

TypeScript

    return Math.sin(deg * Math.PI / 180);
}

    return Math.cos(deg * Math.PI / 180);
}

TypeScript
export function toXY(speed, angle) {
    let x = speed * sinDeg(angle);
    let y = speed * cosDeg(angle);
    return new Vector(x, y);
}

Now you can keep thinking in:

  • 0°

  • 90°

  • 180°

  • 270°

👉 no “hamburger units” required

🧠 Why radians exist (briefly, no suffering)

Radians make math nicer because:

  • derivatives of sin/cos stay clean

  • rotations are proportional to arc length

…but for game dev?

👉 degrees are totally fine and often clearer

⚡ Alternative (cleaner pattern)

If you want to avoid wrapper spam:

const DEG2RAD = Math.PI / 180;

export function toXY(speed, angle) {
    const rad = angle * DEG2RAD;
    return new Vector(
        speed * Math.sin(rad),
        speed * Math.cos(rad)
    );
}

I have got a onPreCollisionResolve, how do I check the target?

ChatGPT said:

In Excalibur.js, the collision callbacks don’t give you a single “target” directly — they give you a collision event object that contains both participants.

So in onPreCollisionResolve, you check the other actor via the contact data.

✅ Basic pattern

TypeScript
onPreCollisionResolve(self, other, side) {
    console.log(other);
}

Depending on your Excalibur version, the signature may instead be:

TypeScript
onPreCollisionResolve(self, other, side, contact) {
    // or just (evt)
}

So the safest approach is to inspect the event object.

🎯 Modern / reliable way (recommended)

Most setups use the event object form:

TypeScript
onPreCollisionResolve(evt) {
    const other = evt.other;
    const self = evt.target;

    console.log('collided with:', other);
}

🧠 What you get in the event

Typically:

TypeScript
evt.target  // this actor
evt.other   // the thing you hit
evt.contact // collision manifold info
evt.side    // collision side (sometimes)

🚨 Example: filter for bullets vs enemies

TypeScript
onPreCollisionResolve(evt) {
    const other = evt.other;

    if (other instanceof Bullet) {
        console.log("hit by bullet");
        this.kill();
    }
}

⚡ Cleaner pattern (recommended architecture)

Instead of checking types everywhere:

Add a tag:

TypeScript
this.tags.add("enemy");

Then:

TypeScript
onPreCollisionResolve(evt) {
    if (evt.other.hasTag("bullet")) {
        this.kill();
    }
}

🧠 Important subtlety

There are multiple collision phases in Excalibur:

EventMeaning
onPreCollisionResolvebefore physics resolves overlap
onPostCollisionafter resolution
onCollisionStartfirst contact

For gameplay (damage, hits), usually prefer:

👉 onCollisionStart

🎯 Recommendation

If you're doing bullets:

TypeScript
onCollisionStart(evt) {
    const other = evt.other;

    if (other instanceof Bullet) {
        this.kill();
        other.kill();
    }
}

If you want, I can help you build a clean collision system (bullets, enemies, player damage) that avoids messy instanceof chains entirely.

ChatGPT said:

This is one of those cases where Excalibur is being consistent, but your two actors are being initialized in slightly different lifecycles, and that difference is enough to break this.on('collisionstart').

Let’s isolate it properly.

🧠 Key fact in Excalibur.js

There are two valid ways collision events are wired:

1. EventEmitter style (what Bubble uses)

TypeScript
this.on('collisionstart', ...)

2. Physics callback style (what Enemy should use in practice)

TypeScript
onCollisionStart(evt) { ... }

Both exist — but they are not equally reliable depending on when the actor enters the world and how its collider is configured.

🚨 Why Bubble works

Your Bubble:

TypeScript
constructor() {
    super({ width: 200, height: 200 })
}

AND:

TypeScript
this.vel = new Vector(500, 0)

AND:

  • simple collider (default)

  • no custom physics constraints

  • no manual collider replacement

  • no damping / DOF modifications

👉 So Excalibur fully initializes it in one clean pipeline

Result:
✔ event system fully attached
✔ this.on is valid
✔ collision events fire normally

🚨 Why Enemy breaks

Your Enemy has ALL of these:

TypeScript
this.collider.set(new CircleCollider(...))
this.body.collisionType = CollisionType.Active
this.body.limitDegreeOfFreedom.push(...)
this.body.useGravity = false
this.body.mass = 1
this.pos = spawnerpos

👉 This combination causes a subtle but important change:

❗ You are manually reconfiguring the physics body BEFORE event binding is finalized

In some Excalibur versions, this means:

the internal event emitter for collision events is NOT attached when this.on() is called in constructor

So:

TypeScript
this.on('collisionstart', ...)

silently fails (no runtime error, just no binding)

🚨 Bubble works because it is “default physics safe”

Enemy is “physics modified early”

That’s the difference.

🧠 The real root cause

Not your logic.

Not tags.

Not collider type.

👉 It is timing of physics body initialization vs event registration

✅ FIX (reliable solution)

Move collision binding to onInitialize

TypeScript
onInitialize(engine) {
    this.on('collisionstart', (e) => {
        const target = e.other.owner;

        if (target?.tags?.has('PLAYERCHARACTER')) {
            target.takeDamage?.();
        }
    });
}

🧠 Why this works

At onInitialize:

✔ physics body fully built
✔ collider registered
✔ event system attached
✔ scene membership resolved

So this.on(...) is guaranteed to exist and work.

🚨 Also: you have a hidden bug

TypeScript
this.addTag('ENEMY')

In Excalibur it is:

TypeScript
this.tags.add('ENEMY');

addTag is not a valid API (Bubble works likely because it never checks enemy tags, so you didn’t notice yet)

🚨 Another issue (important)

You are doing:

TypeScript
this.pos = spawnerpos

This is a shared reference bug again.

Fix:

TypeScript
this.pos = spawnerpos.clone();

🎯 Clean corrected Enemy pattern

TypeScript
export class EnemyBase extends Actor {

    constructor(spawnerpos) {
        super();

        this.pos = spawnerpos.clone();

        this.collider.set(new CircleCollider({ radius: 120 }));

        this.body.collisionType = CollisionType.Active;
        this.body.useGravity = false;
        this.body.mass = 1;

        this.graphics.use(Anims.EnemyDown);

        this.tags.add('ENEMY');

        this.scale = new Vector(0.15, 0.15);
        this.moveTimer = 60;
    }

    onInitialize(engine) {
        this.on('collisionstart', (e) => {
            const target = e.other.owner;

            if (target?.tags?.has('PLAYERCHARACTER')) {
                target.takeDamage?.();
            }
        });
    }
}

🧠 Final explanation in one sentence

Bubble works because it uses default physics + late-safe initialization,
Enemy fails because it modifies the physics body early enough that Excalibur’s collision event wiring is not guaranteed during constructor time.

If you want next step, I can show you a version where:

  • enemies never manually listen to events

  • collision is handled centrally

  • and you get zero lifecycle bugs permanently

That’s the “no more magic failures” architecture.

You said:

despite importing flash, this.flash() returns an error.

ChatGPT said:

That one is simple and a bit anticlimactic: flash() is not an Actor method in Excalibur.

So when you write:

TypeScript
this.flash()

you get an error because there is nothing to call.

🧠 What Excalibur actually provides

In Excalibur.js there is:

  • this.actions (action system)

  • this.graphics (visual system)

  • this.body (physics)

  • this.events / this.on(...)

But no built-in flash() API on Actor.

💡 Why you might think it exists

You likely saw one of these:

1. Custom utility in a tutorial

People often write:

TypeScript
flash() {
    this.actions.blink(100, 100, 5);
}

2. Confusion with Graphics opacity hacks

Like:

TypeScript
this.graphics.opacity = 0.5;

3. Confusion with other engines (Unity-style “flash” helpers)

✅ How to actually “flash” an actor

Option A — blink using actions (best Excalibur-native way)

TypeScript
this.actions.blink(50, 50, 3);

  • duration ON/OFF in ms

  • repeats 3 times

Option B — manual opacity flash

TypeScript
this.graphics.opacity = 0.2;

setTimeout(() => {
    this.graphics.opacity = 1;
}, 100);

Option C — shader/graphic tint flash (advanced)

TypeScript
this.graphics.tint = Color.Red;

then reset later.

🚨 If you thought you imported flash

If you did:

TypeScript
import { flash } from 'excalibur';

That function does not exist in the public API, so:

  • it won’t help

  • bundler may silently ignore it or error elsewhere

🎯 If your goal is “damage feedback flash”

Best pattern:

TypeScript
takeDamage() {
    this.actions.blink(50, 50, 2);
    this.health -= 1;
}

🧠 Key takeaway

There is no missing feature or bug here:

flash() simply does not exist in Excalibur — it’s a common tutorial invention, not a core API.

If you want, I can show you how to build a reusable FlashComponent so every actor can do:

TypeScript
this.flash();

properly (engine-style, not hacky).


You said:

I want to flash the actor white for a few frames

ChatGPT said:

Good, that’s a clean visual feedback requirement. In Excalibur there’s no built-in “flash white” helper, but you can implement it reliably using the graphics tint pipeline, which is what you actually want for sprite-based actors.

✅ Best approach: temporary white tint

In Excalibur.js you can override the sprite color using graphics.tint.

Simple flash (recommended)

TypeScript
import { Color } from 'excalibur';

flashWhite(duration = 100) {
    this.graphics.tint = Color.White;

    setTimeout(() => {
        this.graphics.tint = Color.White; // or reset below
    }, duration);
}

But this is incomplete — because “white tint” alone doesn’t produce a visible flash unless you toggle from a darker tint or store the original.

🎯 Proper implementation (robust)

You want:

  • store original tint

  • set white

  • restore after N ms

TypeScript
import { Color } from 'excalibur';

flashWhite(duration = 80) {
    const original = this.graphics.tint ?? Color.White;

    this.graphics.tint = Color.White;

    setTimeout(() => {
        this.graphics.tint = original;
    }, duration);
}

⚡ Better visual flash (actual “pop” effect)

Pure tinting sometimes looks subtle depending on sprite.

Stronger method = invert brightness via opacity + tint combo

TypeScript
import { Color } from 'excalibur';

flashWhite(duration = 80) {
    const originalTint = this.graphics.tint;
    const originalOpacity = this.graphics.opacity;

    this.graphics.tint = Color.White;
    this.graphics.opacity = 1;

    setTimeout(() => {
        this.graphics.tint = originalTint;
        this.graphics.opacity = originalOpacity;
    }, duration);
}

🧠 Even better (no timers, frame-accurate)

If you want deterministic frame-based flashing (cleaner for gameplay):

TypeScript
flashTimer = 0;

flashWhite(frames = 5) {
    this.flashTimer = frames;
    this.graphics.tint = Color.White;
}

onPreUpdate() {
    if (this.flashTimer > 0) {
        this.flashTimer--;
        if (this.flashTimer === 0) {
            this.graphics.tint = Color.White; // or reset to default
        }
    }
}

🚀 Best practice recommendation

For anything like damage feedback:

✔ use frame-based timer (not setTimeout)
✔ keep a stored “base tint”
✔ reset cleanly in update loop

This avoids:

  • desync with game pause

  • timing drift

  • multi-hit stacking bugs

💡 If you want next step

I can show you a universal DamageFlashComponent so every actor can just do:

TypeScript
this.flash();

with:

  • configurable color

  • stacking protection

  • shader-grade “hit pulse” effect

That’s usually where Excalibur projects start feeling much more polished.


You said:

ive added a ammo variable to the Playercharacter. How would I go about making a hud element to show the current ammo, alongside a scene variable that tracks the score (which increments by killing enemies)

ChatGPT said:

In Excalibur, the clean way to do HUD is: don’t attach it to actors, attach it to the Scene using UI actors or screen-space graphics.

You basically want two things:

  1. A scene-level score variable

  2. A UI Actor (HUD) that reads player + scene state

🧠 1. Score should live on the Scene

In Excalibur.js, scenes are the right place for global run-state.

TypeScript
export class MainScene extends Scene {
    score = 0;

    addScore(amount = 1) {
        this.score += amount;
    }
}

Then from enemies:

TypeScript
this.scene.addScore?.(1);

🎯 2. Ammo stays on the Player

TypeScript
this.ammo = 10;

🧾 3. Create a HUD Actor (screen-space UI)

Excalibur supports UI actors via ScreenElement.

TypeScript
import { ScreenElement, Label, Color, FontUnit } from 'excalibur';

HUD class

TypeScript
export class HUD extends ScreenElement {
    constructor(player, scene) {
        super();

        this.player = player;
        this.sceneRef = scene;

        this.ammoLabel = new Label({
            text: 'Ammo: 0',
            pos: { x: 20, y: 20 },
            color: Color.White,
        });

        this.scoreLabel = new Label({
            text: 'Score: 0',
            pos: { x: 20, y: 50 },
            color: Color.White,
        });

        this.addChild(this.ammoLabel);
        this.addChild(this.scoreLabel);
    }

    onPreUpdate() {
        this.ammoLabel.text = `Ammo: ${this.player.ammo}`;
        this.scoreLabel.text = `Score: ${this.sceneRef.score}`;
    }
}

🎮 4. Add HUD to Scene

In your scene:

TypeScript
onInitialize(engine) {
    this.player = new PC();
    this.add(this.player);

    this.hud = new HUD(this.player, this);
    this.add(this.hud);
}

⚠️ Important detail: ScreenElement vs Actor

  • Actor → exists in world space (moves with camera)

  • ScreenElement → stays on screen (HUD)

So always use:

✔ HUD = ScreenElement

🚀 5. Hook score into enemy kills

In enemy:

TypeScript
onKilled() {
    this.scene?.addScore?.(1);
}

or inside collision:

TypeScript
target.kill();
this.scene.addScore?.(1);

🧠 Cleaner architecture (recommended)

If you want it more scalable:

  • Scene = game state (score, wave, spawn system)

  • Player = local state (ammo, health)

  • HUD = pure renderer (reads state only)

No logic in HUD.

💡 Optional upgrade (better UI system)

Instead of polling in onPreUpdate, you can:

  • update labels only when ammo/score changes

  • or use a small “state store” pattern

You said:

a quick question in between, say I have a class named enemybase which is used for a Seeker enemy to inherit. EnemyBase has constructor(spawnerpos) is this something needed in the seeker constructor as well?

ChatGPT said:

No — not as a separate concept, but you must forward it to super() if the base class expects it.

In JavaScript/TypeScript inheritance (and in Excalibur.js Actors specifically), the rule is:

The child constructor must call super(...) with whatever the parent constructor requires.

🧠 Your case

Base class:

TypeScript
class EnemyBase extends Actor {
    constructor(spawnerPos) {
        super();
        this.pos = spawnerPos;
    }
}

Child class (Seeker)

You do NOT need to re-declare spawnerPos logic, but you DO need to pass it up:

TypeScript
class Seeker extends EnemyBase {
    constructor(spawnerPos) {
        super(spawnerPos); // ✅ required
    }
}

🚨 What happens if you don’t?

If you forget:

TypeScript
constructor(spawnerPos) {
    super(); // ❌ spawnerPos lost
}

Then:

  • EnemyBase never receives the position

  • this.pos = spawnerPos becomes undefined

  • your enemy spawns at (0,0) or breaks physics depending on usage

🧠 When you don’t need anything extra

You only omit parameters in the child if:

1. You want fixed behavior

TypeScript
constructor() {
    super(new Vector(100, 100));
}

2. Or you generate spawn position internally

TypeScript
constructor() {
    super(randomSpawnPoint());
}

🎯 Clean inheritance pattern (recommended)

TypeScript
class EnemyBase extends Actor {
    constructor(spawnerPos) {
        super();
        this.pos = spawnerPos;
    }
}

class Seeker extends EnemyBase {
    constructor(spawnerPos) {
        super(spawnerPos);
    }
}

💡 Key idea

  • Parent defines what data is required

  • Child must either:

    • forward it (super(...))

    • or replace it with its own logic

If you want, I can show you a cleaner pattern where enemies don’t even need constructor arguments at all and instead use a shared spawn(config) factory — it scales much better once you have multiple enemy types.


You said:

another question about inheritance, say I want some enemies to support death effects, if I add if(deathEffect()) { deathEffect() } to the kill segment will that allow for enemies with death effects to play their death effects whilst preventing crashes on enemies that lack a deathEffect method?

ChatGPT said:

Not quite — that pattern won’t reliably do what you want, and it has a couple of logical issues.

🚨 What your code actually does

You proposed:

TypeScript
if (deathEffect()) {
    deathEffect()
}

Problems:

  1. You are calling deathEffect() twice

  2. If deathEffect is undefined, you still crash immediately

  3. The if condition depends on the return value, not existence

So this is not a safe feature check.

🧠 What you actually want

You want:

“If the method exists, call it. Otherwise do nothing.”

That’s a guarded optional method call.

✅ Correct solution (modern JS)

TypeScript
this.deathEffect?.();

That’s it.

In Excalibur.js or plain JS, this means:

  • call deathEffect if it exists

  • otherwise safely skip

🎯 In a kill() method

Example:

TypeScript
kill() {
    this.deathEffect?.();
    super.kill();
}

🧠 Alternative (explicit check)

If you prefer older style:

TypeScript
if (typeof this.deathEffect === "function") {
    this.deathEffect();
}

🚨 Why your version is wrong conceptually

Your version assumes:

TypeScript
if (deathEffect()) { ... }

means “does it exist?”

But it actually means:

“run it and check its return value”

So:

  • if it returns false → block runs incorrectly

  • if it throws → crash before condition even finishes

  • if undefined → immediate error

💡 Best inheritance pattern for your case

For enemies:

TypeScript
class EnemyBase extends Actor {
    kill() {
        this.deathEffect?.();
        super.kill();
    }

    deathEffect() {
        // default = nothing
    }
}

Then override only when needed:

TypeScript
class ExplodingEnemy extends EnemyBase {
    deathEffect() {
        spawnExplosion(this.pos);
    }
}

🧠 Key takeaway

  • Use ?.() for optional behavior

  • Don’t use if (method()) for existence checks

  • Default methods in base class are often cleaner than conditional logic everywhere

If you want next step, I can show you a proper enemy “effect pipeline” (hit flash → stagger → death animation → loot spawn) that scales cleanly without inheritance spaghetti.

ChatGPT said:

That error is misleading, but the cause is very specific.

thePos.clone is not a function

You’re right — you’re not calling .clone() here, but Excalibur is doing it internally, and it’s failing because of how you passed pos.

🚨 The actual problem

This line:

TypeScript
pos: {x:20, y:20}

is not valid for Excalibur UI elements.

In Excalibur.js, pos must be a:

TypeScript
Vector

NOT a plain object.

🧠 What’s happening internally

Excalibur does something like:

TypeScript
this.pos.clone()

But your {x:20, y:20} is just:

TypeScript
{ x: 20, y: 20 } // no .clone() method

→ crash.

✅ Fix

Import Vector and use it properly:

TypeScript
import { ScreenElement, Label, Vector } from 'excalibur'

Then:

TypeScript
this.ammoCounter = new Label({
    text: '',
    pos: new Vector(20, 20),
})

this.scoreCounter = new Label({
    text: '',
    pos: new Vector(20, 50), // also fix overlap
})

🚨 Secondary bug (you stacked them)

You had:

TypeScript
pos: {x:20, y:20}
pos: {x:20, y:20}

So even if it worked, both labels would be on top of each other.

🧠 Small improvement (defensive UI)

This line:

TypeScript
this.scene.PLAYER.ammo

can crash if PLAYER isn’t set yet.

Safer:

TypeScript
this.ammoCounter.text = `BULLETS: ${this.scene?.PLAYER?.ammo ?? 0}`
this.scoreCounter.text = `SCORE: ${this.scene?.score ?? 0}`

🎯 Final corrected UI

TypeScript
import { ScreenElement, Label, Vector } from 'excalibur'

export class UI extends ScreenElement {
    constructor() {
        super()
        
        this.ammoCounter = new Label({
            text: '',
            pos: new Vector(20, 20),
        })

        this.scoreCounter = new Label({
            text: '',
            pos: new Vector(20, 50),
        })

        this.addChild(this.ammoCounter)
        this.addChild(this.scoreCounter)
    }

    onPreUpdate() {
        this.ammoCounter.text = `BULLETS: ${this.scene?.PLAYER?.ammo ?? 0}`
        this.scoreCounter.text = `SCORE: ${this.scene?.score ?? 0}`
    }
}

🧠 Key takeaway

In Excalibur:

Anything spatial (pos, vel, etc.) must be a Vector, not a plain object.

If you want next step, I can show you how to turn this into:

  • animated ammo bar

  • smooth score counter (counts up instead of snapping)

  • hit flash UI feedback

which makes a huge difference in feel.


You said:

How can I make it so that the text size is bigger?

ChatGPT said:

In Excalibur.js, Label text size is controlled via a Font object, not a simple fontSize property like in CSS.

✅ Basic way to increase text size

Import Font and FontUnit:

TypeScript
import { Font, FontUnit } from 'excalibur'

Then assign it to your label:

TypeScript
this.ammoCounter = new Label({
    text: '',
    pos: new Vector(20, 20),
    font: new Font({
        size: 32,          // 👈 this controls size
        unit: FontUnit.Px
    })
})

🎯 Example with both labels

TypeScript
import { ScreenElement, Label, Vector, Font, FontUnit, Color } from 'excalibur'

export class UI extends ScreenElement {
    constructor() {
        super()

        const bigFont = new Font({
            size: 32,
            unit: FontUnit.Px,
            color: Color.White
        })

        this.ammoCounter = new Label({
            text: '',
            pos: new Vector(20, 20),
            font: bigFont
        })

        this.scoreCounter = new Label({
            text: '',
            pos: new Vector(20, 60),
            font: bigFont
        })

        this.addChild(this.ammoCounter)
        this.addChild(this.scoreCounter)
    }
}

🧠 Extra control (useful later)

You can also tweak:

TypeScript
new Font({
    size: 32,
    unit: FontUnit.Px,
    family: 'Arial',
    textAlign: TextAlign.Left,
    baseAlign: BaseAlign.Top,
    color: Color.White
})

⚡ Pro tip

Create the font once and reuse it (like const bigFont = ...), instead of making a new one per label — cleaner and slightly more efficient.

If you want, next step is making:

  • outlined text (so it’s readable on any background)

  • or pixel-font UI that matches your game style

both are very common upgrades after this.
